item.title: [Consumer Psychology #15] The Same Tricks That Sell Can Also Trap: Ethics, Well-Being, and a Full-Course Recap
item.body:
> The psychology that makes marketing work, like attention, memory, and mental shortcuts, can help people choose well or push them into choices they regret. Ethics comes down to which of those two things a design is doing.

## Today's Concept

Over this series we've looked at how consumers notice things, remember them, form attitudes, give in to social pressure, and take mental shortcuts. Here is the short version:

- **Perception and attention:** We only notice a small part of what's around us, so contrast, motion, and novelty get our attention.
- **Memory:** Brands we've seen many times feel familiar, and things that feel familiar tend to feel safe.
- **Attitudes and persuasion:** When we care and have time, we're persuaded by strong arguments. When we're distracted, surface cues like a celebrity, a catchy jingle, or a big number do the work.
- **Social influence:** Reviews, "bestseller" badges, and what our friends buy all signal what's normal.
- **Decision shortcuts (heuristics):** Anchoring, loss aversion, defaults, and scarcity help us decide quickly, and they're also easy to exploit.

Every one of these tools can be used in two ways. A clear label that helps you compare prices uses attention honestly. A countdown timer that resets every time you reload the page uses the same tool to deceive you.

When a design deliberately works against the user's own interests, it's called a **dark pattern**. In a 2022 staff report, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission described dark patterns as design practices that trick or manipulate people into choices they wouldn't otherwise make. Common types include:

- **Roach motel:** Signing up takes one click. Canceling takes a phone call during business hours.
- **Confirmshaming:** The decline button says something like "No thanks, I don't like saving money."
- **Drip pricing:** The advertised price grows as you move toward checkout and fees get added.
- **Fake urgency or scarcity:** "Only 2 left!" or a timer that isn't true.
- **Sneak into basket / pre-checked boxes:** Add-ons you never chose.

The well-being side is about **overconsumption**. Research on materialism and hedonic adaptation shows that the lift from a new purchase usually fades quickly, and we drift back to our baseline mood. Easy credit, one-click checkout, and "buy now, pay later" all make spending feel less painful. That's convenient, but it also makes it easier to spend more than you planned.

## In Everyday Life

Maya, a college student in Ohio, signs up for a streaming service's "free 7-day trial." The page asks for a card number "just to verify." In small gray text it says the plan renews at $15.99/month. Starting the trial takes one button. She forgets about it, and three months later she notices $47.97 on her bank statement.

When she tries to cancel, she has to go through four screens. One says, "Are you sure? You'll lose all your saved shows!" (loss aversion), and another offers "50% off for 2 months" (anchoring plus a retention offer). The cancel link is pale text under a bright "Keep My Plan" button.

None of these tactics is mysterious. Each one is a concept from this course: defaults, inattention, loss aversion, anchoring, and visual salience. An ethical version would use the same psychology to help her. It would send an email reminder before the trial ends, label the price clearly, and offer one-click cancellation.

A quick personal check before buying: *Would I still want this if checkout took 24 hours? Would I sign up if canceling were as hard as this company makes it?*

## 3-Line Summary

1. Consumer psychology tools like attention, memory, social proof, and heuristics are neutral. What makes them ethical or not is whether they help or harm the person deciding.
2. Dark patterns such as roach motels, confirmshaming, drip pricing, and fake scarcity exploit predictable biases to get choices people wouldn't make freely.
3. Purchases give short-lived happiness because of hedonic adaptation, so slowing down and making costs visible protects both your wallet and your well-being.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** A website's "No thanks" button reads, "No, I prefer paying full price." Which dark pattern is this?
- (a) Roach motel
- (b) Confirmshaming
- (c) Drip pricing
- (d) Hedonic adaptation

**Q2. True or False:** Using a default option is always unethical.

**Q3.** A concert ticket is listed at $60, but service and facility fees bring it to $84 at the final step. This is an example of:
- (a) Social proof
- (b) Mere exposure effect
- (c) Drip pricing
- (d) Central-route persuasion

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Dark pattern:** An interface design that steers users toward choices that benefit the company at the user's expense.
- **Roach motel:** A setup where getting into something, like a subscription, is easy and getting out is deliberately hard.
- **Drip pricing:** Showing a low headline price and revealing mandatory fees bit by bit during checkout.
- **Hedonic adaptation:** The tendency to return to a baseline level of happiness after positive (or negative) changes, including new purchases.
- **Choice architecture:** The way options are arranged and presented, which shapes decisions even when no option is removed.

---

*Answers: Q1 (b). Confirmshaming uses guilt or embarrassment to make declining feel bad. Q2 False. Defaults are unavoidable in design, and they can be helpful, like automatic retirement-plan enrollment with an easy opt-out. A default becomes a problem when it's hidden or works against the user's interests. Q3 (c). The real total shows up only at the end, which takes advantage of the effort you've already put in and the anchor of the low first price.*
